title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview at the Capital Compounders Show on February 25, 2025
summary: A relaxed interview covering Pabrai's 2022 move from California to Austin (fires and taxes), his windowless-bedroom library, turning 60, and the four 'games' he plays: bridge, golf, compounding and Dakshana, which he aims to run so that ~$10,000 remains the day before he dies. On investing he reaffirms cloning as 'like breathing' (Sam Walton, Bill Gates, Berkshire's Apple), uses the Nifty-Fifty/Walmart thought experiment to argue that never selling great businesses matters more than error rate, recounts blowing 'trips to the pie counter' on Ferrari and Frontline, and holds Reysas (40x in six years, still undervalued) as the lesson applied.

ideas.idea: I moved from California to Austin in 2022 because of repeated fire evacuations and because California taxes long-term gains as ordinary income, taking about a third of my tax bill.
ideas.detail: Several states have zero income tax (Alaska even pays residents from oil revenue); for most people it boils down to Texas or Florida. Working from his home library raised his productivity and he stopped going to an outside office.

ideas.idea: Everything on the planet is on sale for a price: I quoted a Connecticut couple more than three times what I paid for my house, and being a value guy I would have moved for it.
ideas.detail: Before sending pictures he required they disclose their identities and write a three-paragraph essay on why they would pay two to three times market; they did neither, offered 75% of his ask sight unseen, and he declined.

ideas.idea: Dakshana's aim is the highest social return on invested capital, currently about $3,000 per student on a ~$3 million annual budget for ~1,000 kids a year.
ideas.detail: He knows of no non-profit anywhere delivering a higher social ROIC, but the program cannot absorb more than $6-7 million a year, so at $10-30 million a year he will have to lower the bar and consider other areas such as environment or health.

ideas.idea: Compounding and Dakshana are two math games joined at the hip: one maximizes net worth, the other gives it all away, and played perfectly there should be about $10,000 left the day before I die.
ideas.detail: With just under 30 years of compounding left (MetLife's calculator moved his expected death from 2044 to 2054), the challenge will be on the give-back side as the numbers get larger, not on the compounding side.

ideas.idea: Bridge makes you a better investor because it trains probabilistic thinking: every card played changes the odds and you must recalculate.
ideas.detail: Bridge takes 15 minutes to learn and cannot be mastered in a lifetime, like investing where you never plateau; he played bridge long before investing and found it built the probability muscle. Buffett plays serious duplicate bridge (username T Bone, partner Sharon Osberg) while Munger was a social, bluffing gambler at the table despite being regimented in investing.

ideas.idea: For me cloning is like breathing; humans think it is beneath them or cheating, but the small sliver who go all in on cloning become the best entrepreneurs.
ideas.detail: If you can understand another smart investor's thesis and it is within your circle of competence, that beats figuring everything out yourself; even Berkshire's Apple position came from one of Buffett's two lieutenants and Warren put in 50x their capital. Dakshana itself succeeded only because it cloned a model beyond his pay grade.

ideas.idea: Sam Walton was the ultimate cloner, claiming no one had been inside more non-Walmart retail stores, and he learned from even terrible operators and from blunt truckers.
ideas.detail: He lay on a Brazilian store floor to measure aisle spacing, praised a bad store's candle display, and brought donuts to truckers at 5 a.m. for unfiltered reports on Walmart problems. Bill Gates is another shameless cloner: Word from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus, Windows from Apple, and Bing stands for 'But It's Not Google'.

ideas.idea: Walmart embraced technology very early: Sam Walton flew a small plane to scout the first 50-70 sites between towns and invested heavily in IBM mainframes when Walmart was tiny.
ideas.detail: Managers told him they couldn't run the place without automation, so he stepped up capex; he recommends Made in America.

ideas.idea: You only truly understand a business after you own it, and it can take years of ownership to recognize that you hold a compounder.
ideas.detail: Some businesses like MasterCard or Google are obviously great beforehand, but most are learned from the inside; it took him five or six years to understand Reysas, which has no investor deck and little public data.

ideas.idea: If a 1970s Nifty-Fifty portfolio had put 2% in Walmart at its IPO and the other 98% went to zero, it would still have beaten the S&P over 50 years: investing forgives a 98% error rate, and the key is letting great businesses stay in your portfolio.
ideas.detail: The Nifty-Fifty (Coke, Kodak, Polaroid, Xerox, Colgate, McDonald's) was bought with no price discipline and got 'taken out back and shot' in 1973-74, with Coke down to ~6x earnings, yet the one Walmart would have carried everything.

ideas.idea: Selling great businesses because of valuation is one of the dumbest things you can do, and I did it repeatedly, most painfully with Ferrari.
ideas.detail: In 2012 Fiat Chrysler had a $5-6 billion market cap and he invested $50-60 million for ~1%; that stake included 80% of Ferrari, now worth $90 billion, so doing nothing would have left a ~$900 million position against his ~$1 billion of total assets, versus the ~$150 million he captured.

ideas.idea: The Walton family went from 38% of Walmart at the 1970-71 IPO to 44% today by simply holding while the company bought back stock, paying no frictional costs or taxes.
ideas.detail: Sam Walton gave the shares to his kids before the IPO (no estate tax), has been dead ~30 years, no Waltons run the company, and they ignored the 'helpers' urging diversification.

ideas.idea: Munger told me 'you only need to get rich once'; trying to optimize compounding is a mistake that blew up in my face, and once you know you hold a compounder you sell only on true secular decline, never on valuation.
ideas.detail: Not a down quarter, a wiggle or a recession, but a genuine secular decline in the business is the only worthy reason to consider selling.

ideas.idea: Munger's pie counter: you get only three or four trips in a lifetime, so load up on a lot of pie and keep it; I blew trips on Ferrari and on Frontline, which I sold after a double and which became a 70x in three years.
ideas.detail: Every few months Munger would recite the same successful trips (Berkshire, Costco, Li Lu, apartment houses) and was content if there were no more; with 30 years left Pabrai hopes for two or three more trips but says the pies already held cannot be let go.

ideas.idea: Reysas cost about $8 million for a third of the company nearly six years ago when everyone was exiting Turkey; it is up ~40x in dollars to a billion-plus market value and is still undervalued with a liquidation value around $2 billion.
ideas.detail: Unlike Ferrari at 50x trailing earnings, there is no need to scratch his head; having taken the arrows with Ferrari, the rule is simply to hang on until the business goes to hell. Every trip to Turkey still surprises him because so little about the business is public.

ideas.idea: You can't tell in advance which one of ten holdings is the Walmart, but if you own them all and don't mess with the ones with great economics and management, you will be fine.
ideas.detail: Buffett made 400-500 investments over 70-75 years and said 12 moved the needle; one of the 12 was hiring Ajit Jain, whose sub-$100,000 search fee created a couple hundred billion dollars of value, which Munger called Berkshire's highest-return investment.

ideas.idea: Extreme concentration is the natural outcome of successful investing: keep your winners and the best will become 70-90% of the portfolio, as Berkshire did for Buffett and Munger.
ideas.detail: Steve Ballmer, a hired gun whose CEO tenure returned ~4% a year, now has a net worth exceeding Bill Gates because his portfolio is essentially Microsoft plus some S&P and he never sold, and he put Satya Nadella in place.

ideas.idea: Cannibals remain a tremendous mental model: a great business buying back shares at modest valuations turbocharges returns without dividend tax leakage, but buybacks at a bad business or high price incinerate wealth.
ideas.detail: Walmart's buybacks raised the Walton stake even as they sold shares for charity; Eddie Lampert's Sears buybacks were a great way to destroy wealth. Both conditions, great business and non-overpaying price, must hold.

ideas.idea: The best things in life are free: all chapters of my out-of-print first book Mosaic are posted as free PDFs on my blog, even though used copies sell for $500-800.
ideas.detail: He posted them specifically to bring the resale price down; The Dhandho Investor remains his better-known book.
